Known limitations - OpenContent has been retired : space and member management, upload and download, and native documents are no longer served by an OpenContent Provider. The capabilities remain registered, but they fail closed when no Provider is available. - The current SiYuan Provider declares notebook discovery only; other operations return blocked_by_contract . The local mock Provider is for testing only and is not a user feature. - The readiness level is evidence only and does not guarantee that a given call will be allowed. Every call also checks the current identity, authorization, audience, platform, transfer limits, and binding status. - Immutable artifact references ( ArtifactReference ) require proof of immutable retention and exact-version reads. Issuance is blocked when those conditions are not currently met. - Shared container members and Cloud Project members are two separate identity boundaries. Provider membership does not grant Project permissions. Related pages - SiYuan Notes: the currently installed Content Space Provider and its capability boundaries. - Collaboration: the relationship between the Cloud Drive section and delivery files. - Permissions and security: general rules for external writes and per-operation confirmation. - Feature status and limitations: how current capability status is defined. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-content-space v5.0.4.

en.title: Create Loop (multi-step workflows)
en.description: Chain AI, conditions, HTTP, and human approvals in multi-node workflows.
en.body: Create Loop (multi-step workflows) Create Loop breaks a task into multiple inspectable steps. It sits above session execution: AI nodes generate or decide, condition and data-processing nodes control the path, HTTP nodes connect external systems, subflows reuse another Loop, and human approvals determine whether key actions proceed. The feature status table lists this plugin as Verified . How to open it - Entry: Create Loop at the top of the workbench. Edit nodes on the canvas; the right panel shows settings for the current Loop. - Target: one Loop in the current workspace. Definitions and run records are stored in local domain state. - Prerequisite: AI nodes need an available Runtime and model, HTTP nodes need network access, and schedules and local webhooks are triggered by the app process, so the app must remain running. A Loop can be started with manual Run once , a schedule, a webhook, or an Agent hook. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Chain a multi-step task Add AI agent task , LLM generation , Condition , HTTP request , human approval, subflow, and other nodes from the left node panel, then connect them A Loop you can save Branch on data Organize inputs and outputs with Condition, Switch, Merge, Filter, Loop, and similar nodes Explicit data flow between nodes Validate before going live Use Test node with mock upstream input for a single node, then Run once for the whole Loop Node results and run logs Stop at key points Add a Human Approval node, set the title, instruction, and timeout, then Approve/Reject on the card or in the run drawer Controlled release Trigger automatically Configure a schedule, webhook, or Agent hook Scheduled, external, or event-driven triggers Typical workflow 1. Open Create Loop at the top, name it, and confirm the working directory. AI, image, and code nodes all use that directory. 2. Add trigger and task nodes and connect them in execution order. Write clear input references, error handling, and timeouts for each node. 3. Use Test node with mock upstream input to validate a single node first. The current Loop is saved before testing. 4. Click Run once and check each node's input, output, timing, and errors in the Run log , Run history , and Audit report . 5. After validation, turn on Enabled , enable AI-callable as needed, configure schedules or webhooks, and keep human approvals before key steps. Figure 1: The Create Loop canvas connects multiple processing nodes into a runnable flow. Select a node to inspect its parameters on the right. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: workspace files, upstream node output, Loop definitions, run history, and approval status. - Writes: Loop definitions are stored in local domain state; nodes can write to the workspace; each run saves a run Manifest and per-node receipts and provides an audit report. - Approval or external effects: starting an entire flow, stopping a run, and handling approvals are governed as external writes and require confirmation. HTTP and AI nodes make real requests and incur costs. - What it does not do: write raw Secret values to run records, restore paused approvals after the app restarts, or approve on a person's behalf. Known limitations - Human approval pause state is held in memory, and an app restart loses that run. Important flows should make nodes repeatable and keep idempotency keys. - Schedules and webhooks depend on the app process. They do not fire while the app is closed. - Secret variables store only the slot and fingerprint. When a Secret is required and no safe replay resolution is available, execution blocks rather than continuing with an empty value. - A single-node test proves only that node, not the whole flow. Tests also execute the node logic for real. - When randomness is not fixed, rerun differences are marked as indeterminate and cannot be treated directly as a reproduction failure. Related pages - Automation and scheduled tasks: scheduled execution of a single AI instruction, and when to use Create Loop instead. - Evidence & Reproducibility: run records, artifact versions, and the evidence chain. - Agent workflows: Agent hooks and execution boundaries in sessions. - Permissions and security: external requests, writes, and confirmation rules. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-create-loop v1.1.4.

en.title: Dataset API
en.description: Register data sources, fetch public biological data with validation, and produce reproducible datasets.
en.body: Dataset API Dataset API is the workspace-level data ingestion and preparation layer: it registers public biological databases, private object storage, and derived datasets as governable data sources, then uses plan-based flows to fetch, organize, validate, and publish them. Use it for the "find data, fetch data, turn it into a reproducible dataset" stage, together with Life Science Preview and Create Loop. Opening it - Entry point: the dataset result card in a session; the Create Loop resource panel. Custom endpoints and object storage connections can only be registered through the UI, and they require confirmation. - Applies to: the current workspace and its .sciforge/datasets data source registry. - Prerequisite: the data source address is reachable; when authentication is needed, reference credentials through environment variables; S3-compatible storage requires registering the service address, bucket, and allowed prefixes first. What it can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Find public biological data sources Browse the bundled biological provider catalog and check metadata, raw data endpoints, and authentication requirements Catalog entries with an explanation of the adaptation approach Fetch metadata or raw data Issue a size-limited request against a registered endpoint, choosing metadata or raw data Derived files with SHA-256, a provenance manifest, and a request receipt, plus fragment previews Browse object storage After registering S3-compatible storage, list objects, read object headers, and download by range Object copies named by checksum, with metadata Prepare data on a plan Generate a preparation plan, review and confirm it, then execute Immutable plans, run checkpoints, derived datasets, and provenance manifests Validate quality and publish Run validation, then publish Reproducible dataset versions and data-construction-pipeline.md What it does not do: it does not run arbitrary shell, SQL, or Python, and it does not treat model-generated code as processing logic. Every preparation step is carried out deterministically by Dataset API from strict JSON parameters; failures should be retried or recovered through Dataset API, not worked around by connecting directly with curl in the terminal. Typical workflow 1. Pick a provider in the catalog and confirm the endpoint, authentication method, and adaptation type; do not assume an adapter is implemented just from a catalog entry. 2. Register custom endpoints or object storage through the UI; the Agent cannot add arbitrary endpoints and can only use registered source IDs. 3. Fetch metadata or raw data, then verify checksums, byte ranges, and source receipts. 4. Generate a preparation plan, review the data-construction pipeline that comes with it, then confirm and execute. 5. On failure, resume with the immutable plan ID and run ID; when done, run validation, and before publishing confirm that the validation report covers the same path and SHA-256. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Read: the workspace data source registry, public catalogs, registered API responses, and object storage objects. - Write: registry, run state, derived artifacts with checksums, provenance manifests, and published versions; source files are not overwritten. - Approval or external effects: custom endpoint and object storage registration, and plan confirmation, require confirmation; registering preset providers, ordinary fetches, and preparation run as workspace write. - What it will not do: store credentials in plaintext, execute arbitrary code, turn generic sources into an arbitrary URL proxy, or silently overwrite existing content. Known limitations - Catalog entries describe access methods only and do not mean the corresponding adapter is implemented. - Requests to generically registered sources allow GET only, subject to timeouts, response size, cross-origin redirects, and HTTPS restrictions; the only exception is the whitelisted UniProt ID mapping POST. - Object storage currently uses the S3-compatible API: listings return at most 1,000 keys per page, and downloads default to a 256 MiB cap; HTTPS is on by default, and internal HTTP requires explicit confirmation. - Public database availability, rate limits, and field changes are outside SciForge's control; failures come back as structured receipts. - Raw downloads are stored byte for byte, without parsing or converting source data; hand scientific interpretation to a preview or analysis step. Related pages - Life Science Preview: view fetched sequence, structure, imaging, and other files. - Biology Room: organize fetched biological files into an annotatable room. - Permissions and security: approvals, credentials, and external access boundaries. - Feature status and limitations: the current capability stance. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-dataset-api v1.0.2.

en.title: Evidence & Reproducibility
en.description: Use artifact versions, Checkpoints, Evidence DAG, and Research Dossier to fix the research process and results.
en.body: Evidence & Reproducibility Once a research task is finished, a summary that looks correct is not the same as a reproducible deliverable. SciForge uses several complementary objects to record what happened, what was produced, what it rests on, and where to continue next time. This group consists of 7 independent plugins, each responsible for one kind of record; this page only explains how they connect: Plugin Record it owns --- --- Artifact Versions Immutable versions of a single artifact, comparison, and restore Git Checkpoints A Git snapshot of the workspace at a given stage Research Checkpoints The context and resume point of one research stage Change Inspector The list of files a session actually changed Evidence DAG How claims relate to sources, methods, figures, and limitations within a session Project DAG Project-level goals, claims, and review status across sessions Research Dossier The final research deliverable for other people Choose the right record object Object Problem it solves Typical content --- --- --- Session How did the task progress? Messages, tool calls, commands, approvals, and the final answer Artifact Version How did a chart or file evolve? Artifact paths, versions, inputs, and generation information Git Checkpoint What stage are the workspace files at? Git status and stage-level code snapshots Research Checkpoint How do I continue a research stage? Research context, key artifacts, and resume point Evidence DAG What supports or refutes a claim? Claims, sources, methods, artifacts, limitations, and relationships Research Dossier How do others read the final deliverable? Research question, inputs, methods, results, credibility, and limitations Build an auditable chain Recommended order: 1. Record the workspace, input versions, and goal at the start of the task. 2. After key computations, save the commands, parameters, and artifacts. 3. Create artifact versions for figures or reports. 4. Link key claims to inputs, methods, and figures. 5. Check counterevidence, missing data, and inference boundaries by hand. 6. Save a Checkpoint and generate a Research Dossier. Figure 1: The research dossier shows the research narrative, the current version, the credibility summary, and the limitations that need attention. Have the agent leave a complete record You can add this to the task: After finishing the analysis, put the research question, input files, methods used, key parameters, results, and limitations into the research dossier. Every key conclusion should trace back to the corresponding source, derived table, or figure; mark anything you cannot confirm as unverified. Don't just ask for "generate an Evidence DAG". First be clear about which claims are worth reviewing, which data can support them directly, and which interpretations are still candidate hypotheses. Manual review checklist - Can every key number be traced back to an input file and computation step? - Do the figures come from verified derived tables rather than manually edited intermediate files? - Do the conclusions conflate correlation, prediction, and causation? - Are counterevidence, warnings, and missing data still visible? - Are the code commit, environment, parameters, and random seed needed to re-run all present? - Does the Checkpoint correspond to a Git state that has been checked? Data boundaries Evidence DAG and Research Dossier show meaningful content only when the current workspace and session already have the corresponding data. An empty panel does not mean the feature is broken; first have the task produce explicit claims, sources, and artifact records. Case: ECCITE-seq cross-scale virtual cell evidence map.

en.title: Evidence DAG
en.description: Connect claims in a session to their sources, methods, artifacts, and limitations.
en.body: Evidence DAG Evidence DAG is the evidence compiler inside a session: it extracts claims, sources, runs, artifacts, and relationships from the visible runtime trace, and compiles them into an immutable evidence snapshot on an explicit update or at a formal boundary. It answers “what supports or refutes this conclusion?” It sits after a single analysis and before project-level aggregation and external delivery; cross-session aggregation is handled by Project DAG. How to open it - Entry: the Evidence DAG panel on the right; resource navigation from a Claim, an evidence snapshot, or a similar item opens the corresponding session. - Target: committed evidence snapshots in the current Runtime and session. - Prerequisite: the task has produced a compilable trace, and the Evidence service and text-reasoning configuration are available. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Leave a reviewable trace Run the task normally; tool results declare evidenceLineage Runtime trace increments Generate a new snapshot Click Update and wait for queueing and commit to finish An immutable Evidence snapshot Inspect claims and evidence Select a node in the graph to view its sources, runs, artifacts, and relationships The in-session evidence graph Check provenance breakpoints Review provenance coverage, breakpoints, and limitation notes A list of evidence gaps Run a structure audit Click Audit to run a read-only check against the committed snapshot L0 audit results Download a rerun spec Select a Conclusion node and click Download rerun spec A .sciforge-rerun.json file Typical workflow 1. Complete a round of analysis and make sure tool results carry structured lineage and exact artifact references. 2. Click Update and confirm the status moves from queued to running and then to committed. 3. Check the full chain from claim to source, run, code, environment, and artifact version. 4. Manually confirm breakpoints such as a missing source, an unverified version, or a missing approval; do not paper over them with prose explanations. 5. When you need a cross-session, project-level view, move on to the Project DAG. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: runtime traces visible to the current session, tool receipts, committed snapshots, Artifact versions, and source anchors. - Writes: evidence delta storage, immutable snapshots, and the audit sidecar; rerun specs are exported from committed snapshots. - Approval or external effects: updating needs no extra approval, but it writes evidence state and snapshots and calls the configured text-reasoning service; downloading a rerun spec is read-only. Rebuilding is an advanced operation and requires specifying a reason and writing a justification. - What it does not do: promote chat summaries or raw tool receipts directly to scientific artifacts, infer missing metadata from prose, or rewrite committed snapshots. Known limitations - Feature status is Partially available : the entry is registered, but the graph only becomes meaningful once a task actually produces claims, sources, and artifact records; an empty panel is not a failure. - Only nodes and edges in committed snapshots are audit-eligible; pending failures are shown separately and never make the committed graph unusable. - Promoting a claim to L4 requires a stable run record, verifiable inputs, exact software, parameters, environment, and logs or artifacts; stochastic runs must also supply a random seed. - Missing fields become named provenance breakpoints and are never filled in by inference; the built-in audit currently performs deterministic L0 structural checks. - Rebuilding is only for schema upgrades, corruption recovery, or reinterpretation, not a routine editing entry point; previews of restricted evidence fail according to the access policy. Related pages - Evidence & Reproducibility: the group overview and the recommended record chain. - Project DAG: aggregate the committed snapshots of several sessions into a project view. - Research Dossier: the reading-oriented delivery surface. - Artifact Versions: the immutable artifact versions that evidence references. - Virtual cell evidence atlas case: how evidence is organized in a complete task. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-evidence-dag v1.1.5.

en.title: Skills, MCP, and Extensions
en.description: Distinguish bundled domains, locally signed extensions, Agent Skills, and MCP Servers, and enable them safely.
en.body: Skills, MCP, and Extensions An “extension” in SciForge is not a single mechanism. Understanding the object types keeps documentation methods, external tools, and in-app panels from being confused with one another. Extension Center Open Extensions in the left sidebar to view bundled domain extensions, locally installed packages, and Skills. Extension details should show the source, publisher, version, status, and contributions. Figure 1: Extension Center distinguishes bundled from locally installed extensions and shows contributions such as panels, toolbar actions, previews, and Agent capabilities. Local extensions accept only official SciForge-signed packages. Installation verifies the complete file set, Ed25519 signature, publisher identity, and Host API. Workspace content never installs or executes extensions automatically. Extension Marketplace The Marketplace page in Extension Center uses the index bundled with the app, and a deployment can point it to a remote index. The installation chain performs permission confirmation, download, size and SHA-256 verification, publisher signature verification, staged unpacking, and atomic replacement in order. If any step fails, the existing installation is left intact. - Before installation, the plugin's declared capabilities are listed and the user must confirm before continuing. - Installed plugins can be disabled, enabled, or uninstalled. After uninstall, the corresponding capabilities are removed from the host immediately. - Entries that are not published or are blocked state the reason, such as undeclared tools, capabilities that conflict with a built-in plugin, or a failed build. - Whether a Marketplace entry can be installed depends on the current in-app index. This does not change the bundled domain extensions listed in this chapter. Agent Skill Skills are specialized methods and workflows for Codex or Claude Code, usually consisting of SKILL.md plus supporting scripts and reference materials. Before enabling one, read: - The Skill's trigger conditions and scope - Whether it runs scripts, accesses the network, or writes files - Required software, data, and credentials - How results are verified Figure 2: The Skills page is used to view, create, and manage project-level or global Skills. Recognition of a Skill does not mean its scripts have been executed automatically. Installation, dependencies, and scripts from third-party Skills still require independent review. MCP Server An MCP Server provides external tools or data to the Agent. When configuring one, record at least: - The source and version of the service - The launch command or service address - The environment variables used and the credential scope - Whether tools read local files, write to external systems, or send data - Whether failures are retried, and how duplicate writes are avoided Writes, sends, uploads, or deletes in external systems should not be authorized automatically just because MCP is connected. Computer Use Backend Computer Use lets supported Runtimes operate desktop apps. It also requires a local Backend, screen recording, and Accessibility permissions. Limit the target apps and task scope, and require user confirmation before key actions such as signing in, authorizing, paying, sending, or deleting. Figure 3: The Settings page shows Runtime access, Backend status, and macOS permissions separately. Troubleshooting order 1. Confirm that the extension or Skill status is not “Restart required” or “Invalid.” 2. Start a new session so the Runtime rediscovers available capabilities. 3. Check the target workspace, Skill directory, and MCP configuration. 4. Look for explicit errors in tool calls; do not rely on silent fallbacks. 5. For local extensions, verify the signature, Host API, and version. Related page: Permissions and security.

en.title: Git Checkpoints
en.description: Pin Git state at task-turn boundaries and capture a rescue snapshot automatically before any restore.
en.body: Git Checkpoints Git Checkpoints record a Git snapshot of the workspace before and after a task turn, pinning down “what state the code was in when this round started and when it finished.” It owns only checkpoint metadata and restore policy; actual repository operations run through the generic version-control capability. Research context itself is recorded by Research Checkpoints. How to open it - Entry: Git Checkpoints in the top toolbar; the right panel is titled Git Checkpoints as well. - Target: the local Git workspace bound to the current session. - Prerequisite: the workspace is a Git repository and a version-control provider is available; a non-Git workspace never produces checkpoints. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Review turn checkpoints Open the panel and read the records before and after each turn by time A checkpoint list with phases Check the scope of changes Select a checkpoint to view the workspace patch and change summary A diff preview Restore a known state Select the target checkpoint, click Restore , and confirm A workspace back at that snapshot Avoid losing state on restore No extra step; the system captures it automatically before restoring A rescue checkpoint ID Refresh the current list Click the refresh icon to reload The latest checkpoint list Typical workflow 1. Start a task in a Git workspace; the system records a checkpoint before the turn. 2. After the turn completes or ends, refresh the panel and confirm the after-turn checkpoint appears. 3. Select the target checkpoint, review the patch preview first, and then decide whether to restore. 4. When you need to restore, click Restore and confirm, and wait while the system creates a rescue checkpoint first. 5. After the restore finishes, recheck the workspace state and the Changes panel. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: workspace Git state, snapshot metadata, patches, and change summaries. - Writes: checkpoint metadata is written to the application data directory; restoring rewrites workspace files. - Approval or external effects: restoring is destructive and requires explicit confirmation; if the rescue checkpoint cannot be created, the restore is aborted. - What it does not do: run Git commands directly or bypass version-control provider policy, or fabricate checkpoints in a non-Git workspace. Known limitations - The current implementation covers turn-boundary checkpoints for local Git workspaces; the panel provides listing, preview, refresh, and restore. - The panel has no button for creating checkpoints by hand; checkpoints are triggered by the turn lifecycle and do not depend on the panel staying open or on manual saves. - A patch preview may be truncated by the version-control provider, in which case only part of the diff is visible. - Restoring is a workspace-level rollback, not a read-only comparison; the rescue checkpoint is a protection point captured automatically before the restore. - It does not store the research question, sources, or restore position, so it cannot replace a Research Checkpoint. Related pages - Evidence & Reproducibility: the group overview and the recommended record chain. - Research Checkpoints: save research context and the restore position. - Artifact Versions: pin a single artifact instead of the whole workspace. - Change Inspector: check which files one session actually changed. - Workspaces and sessions: how workspaces, sessions, and Git state relate. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-git-checkpoints v1.0.3.

en.title: Identity & Access
en.description: Manage local attribution and cloud identity separately, with clear boundaries for sign-in, device authorization, and revocation.
en.body: Identity & Access Identity & Access answers “who is acting now, and is this device authorized?” It does not participate in specific research analysis, but it determines whether external capabilities such as Collaboration and Content Space can act on behalf of the current user. How to open it - Entry: the Account area at the top of the workbench. It opens the Identity panel, which is divided into “Local account” and “SciForge Cloud.” - Target: the current installation, current local account, current Desktop device, and cloud sign-in session. - Prerequisite: local features do not require sign-in. Cloud sign-in requires the SciForge Cloud address provided by your administrator, an account, and a working system browser. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Mark the local user Create or select a local account, and rename it if needed A local attribution marker that is restored automatically after a restart Sign in to the cloud In “SciForge Cloud,” click Browser sign-in and complete OIDC sign-in in the system browser The current cloud user and sign-in session Authorize this device After signing in, click Connect this device to complete Desktop device registration An active device that can access cloud capabilities End or transfer authorization Use Sign out or Disconnect this device Local features remain, while cloud and cross-user permissions are revoked immediately Typical workflow 1. Open Account at the top and create or select a local account. It is used only for local attribution and does not need to match your cloud name. 2. Click Browser sign-in and complete account authentication in the system browser. Do not paste your password or token back into SciForge. 3. After returning, click Connect this device and confirm that the panel shows both signed-in status and “This device is connected.” 4. When you leave, change machines, or lose a device, sign out first. Disconnect the device only when you are sure it will no longer be used. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: the local account list, current cloud user, device connection status, and session validity. - Writes: local account selection and display name, OIDC sign-in sessions, and device registration and revocation. Project content is never written. - Approval or external effects: browser sign-in and device registration change cloud account state. Signing out and disconnecting a device immediately affect features that depend on cloud identity, so they require user confirmation. - Credentials: OIDC refresh material, the device signing private key, and Agent authorization are stored only in platform private storage (macOS Keychain, Windows DPAPI, Linux libsecret/KWallet). If secure storage is unavailable, the operation fails closed. - What it does not do: treat a local account as security authentication, isolate local data, fill in passwords on your behalf, or expose tokens to the interface or other domain packages. Known limitations - A local account is only an attribution marker. Workspaces, settings, and API keys on the same installation are not isolated when you switch local accounts. - Completing sign-in does not mean the device is registered. Cross-user permissions require both a cloud-authenticated identity ( cloud-authenticated Principal) and an ACTIVE device. Device registration is more like a lease that must stay valid rather than a one-time permanent authorization. - If the device is revoked, a refresh is unconfirmed, or the OIDC user changes, the cloud-authenticated identity immediately falls back to local selection, and capabilities that depend on it, such as Collaboration, stop. - Signing out usually keeps the device registration. To revoke this device's ability to access the cloud, choose Disconnect this device . - If platform secure storage is missing or insecure, SciForge refuses to save credentials. There are no environment variables, plaintext files, or other fallback paths. - The email address, display name, or membership of an external account is not treated as SciForge identity. Binding an external account must be explicit and revocable. Related pages - Collaboration: cloud sign-in and an active device are prerequisites for multi-user collaboration. - Content Space: Provider connections bind to the current identity, and switching accounts invalidates old bindings. - Permissions and security: general rules for approvals, credentials, and data boundaries. - Remote resources and collaboration: the differences between remote workspaces, Cloud sign-in, and device registration. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-identity-access v5.0.2.

en.title: Life Science Preview
en.description: View structure, sequence, omics, imaging, and spectral files directly in the workspace.
en.body: Life Science Preview Life Science Preview routes common scientific files to dedicated views, so you can confirm what an object contains in file preview before deciding whether to hand it to an Agent for analysis. It sits in the "read data" stage and works alongside Biology Room, which organizes sample objects, and Dataset API, which fetches public data. Opening it - Entry point: file preview in the file panel; open a supported local or remote workspace file. - Applies to: workspace files; the extension and the preview manifest select the matching view. - Prerequisite: the file is in the current workspace; remote workspaces are read by the remote Workspace Host, and the UI does not require downloading the whole file locally first. What it can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- View molecular structures Open .pdb , .cif , .mmcif , .sdf , .mol , .mol2 , .xyz Chain, residue, and ligand summaries; a Mol view; distance, angle, or dihedral measurements when coordinates are available View sequences and genomes Open .fasta , .fa , .fna , .faa , .fastq , .gb , .gbk , .gff , .gff3 , .gtf , .bed , .vcf Record counts, lengths, features, intervals, variant summaries, and region selection View omics matrices Open .h5ad , .loom , .mtx , .h5 , .hdf5 , .zarr Matrix dimensions, observation/variable keys, embedding names, and metadata summaries View bioimages Open .tif , .tiff , .ome.tif , .ome.tiff , .czi , .svs , .ndpi Dimensions, channels, OME metadata, region of interest (ROI) and channel selection; thumbnails and tiles for TIFF/OME-TIFF View spectral and proteomics data Open .mzml , .mzxml , .mgf , .fcs Scan/event summaries, peak counts, intensity ranges, sampled peaks, and peak-interval annotations Carry companion indexes Open .fai , .gzi , .tbi , .csi Transferred as companion indexes for sequence or genome files, for later object references What it does not parse: omics files are read as metadata only; HDF5, AnnData, Loom, and Zarr matrices are not decoded; CZI, SVS, and NDPI provide only container metadata placeholders, with no pixel decoding; FCS focuses on the visible header, keywords, and sampled-peak summary and does not provide a full event matrix; trajectory and density files can be handed to the Mol view, but they fall outside chain, residue, and ligand summary parsing. Preview is a reading aid, not validation-grade format parsing or an analysis tool. Typical workflow 1. Confirm the workspace location at the top, then open the target file in the file panel. 2. Check the format, size, dimensions, or record count in the preview to confirm you opened the right file. 3. To continue analysis, create a region, residue, or channel selection so the Agent works on the original file. 4. In a remote workspace, confirm first that reads happen on the remote side; do not ask the Agent to copy a large file just for preview. 5. Treat preview results as session context only; key conclusions should still go back to the original files and compute records. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Read: preview summaries read the beginning of the file, at most 2 MB for text and 4 MB for binary, with an explicit truncation marker beyond that; the Workspace Host that owns the data performs the read. - Write: preview itself does not modify source files; export only copies a same-format source file to a new workspace path. - Approval or external effects: opening and reading need no approval; exporting a copy requires confirmation and writes to a new workspace path. - What it will not do: convert formats, repair corrupted files, treat a preview summary as complete data, or upload workspace files. Known limitations - Observation lists are truncated with an explicit marker, and oversized selections are rejected. - Omics matrices, proprietary imaging containers, and FCS are metadata or placeholder previews and cannot support quantitative analysis. - Bioimage thumbnails and tiles are attempted only for TIFF/OME-TIFF; compressed or non-8-bit TIFFs may fall back to metadata. - Sequence and genome previews are based on truncated text and cannot replace full format validation or variant calling. - Unregistered extensions do not enter these dedicated views and are handled as ordinary workspace files. Related pages - Biology Room: organize multiple sequences, structures, and annotations into a traceable room. - Dataset API: fetch validated data from public biological databases and object storage. - Workbench tools: how files, the terminal, the browser, and other entry points divide the work. - Feature status and limitations: the current stance on each capability. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-life-science-preview v1.0.1.

en.title: Features & Extensions overview
en.description: Browse SciForge bundled domain extensions plugin by plugin — from sources and analysis to evidence and collaboration, one page each.
en.body: Features & Extensions overview SciForge ships 22 bundled domain extensions with the installer. Each one owns its capabilities, UI entry points, and permission boundaries as an independent plugin, and all of them are listed together in the Extension Center. This chapter devotes one page to each plugin, describing its entry points, what it can do, what it produces, and its current limitations. It refers to bundled domain extensions compiled with the app that need no separate download (trusted compile-time). Locally installed packages, Agent Skills, and MCP Servers in the Extension Center are three other kinds of object; see Skills, MCP, and Extensions. The Extension Center shows bundled domain extensions, locally installed packages, and Skills separately, and labels each with its source, version, and status. Find plugins by research stage Research sources and scientific objects Plugin What it solves Main entry point --- --- --- Life Science Preview View sequence, structure, omics, spectral, and imaging files directly in the workspace, without converting them to text first File preview Dataset API Register public biological databases and object storage, pull and organize data on a plan, and retain provenance Session result card, Create Loop resource panel Biology Room Organize biological experiments, samples, and run records into workspace objects you can keep working with Workspace file preview, capability invocation Scientific Compute Run governed compute steps through a deterministic local Provider Capability invocation Analysis and review Plugin What it solves Main entry point --- --- --- Scientific Figures Select files, plot through chat, link Python code and runs, and compare and formally accept candidates "Scientific Figures" in the right sidebar (local MVP) Visual Review Review images and charts by hand and route feedback explicitly back to the Agent Right panel Anchored Comments Anchor comments to files, text positions, or selections so people and the Agent share them Top toolbar, global overlay Evidence & Reproducibility Plugin What it solves Main entry point --- --- --- Artifact Versions Save immutable versions of a single artifact, compare differences, and restore as a new version Research dossier panel (research summary) Git Checkpoints Pin the Git state of a workspace at a given stage so you can return to a known baseline Right panel, top toolbar Research Checkpoints Save the context and resume point of a research stage so the next session has a footing Session result card Change Inspector Summarize which files a session actually changed, instead of going by the Agent's summary alone Right panel, top toolbar Evidence DAG Connect claims from a session to sources, methods, figures, and limitations Right panel Project DAG Aggregate project-level goals, claims, review status, and decisions across sessions Right panel Research Dossier Turn research questions, inputs, methods, results, and limitations into an external-facing deliverable Right panel Agent and workbench tools Plugin What it solves Main entry point --- --- --- Terminal Run commands in a controlled workspace and keep the commands and output Bottom panel, top toolbar Browser Preview Open web pages inside the app and let the Agent operate them under explicit approval Right panel Computer Use Let supported Runtimes operate desktop apps through a local Backend MCP, system permissions Automation Plugin What it solves Main entry point --- --- --- Create Loop Chain AI tasks, conditions, HTTP, approvals, and subflows in a multi-node flow Top toolbar, right panel Collaboration and content Plugin What it solves Main entry point --- --- --- Identity & Access Manage local accounts, OIDC sign-in, device registration, and credential boundaries Top account entry point Collaboration Let several people divide work in a project, claim tasks, review, and deliver results Main workspace Content Space Upload, download, and open native documents in a Provider content space Right panel SiYuan Notes Connect your own remote SiYuan service as a full-page editor and archive task summaries automatically Main workspace How to choose - Start with sources : if a file will not open or you cannot read its format, start with Life Science Preview. - Get data first : if you need a public database or object storage, register the source with Dataset API, then have the Agent work from that source. - Plot something : use Scientific Figures to generate, modify, and accept candidates through chat, with code and run records linked and saved inside the plugin. Visual Review and Artifact Versions are separate capabilities; check each one's scope before use. - Deliver : solidify the work in the order "Change Inspector → checkpoints → Evidence DAG → research dossier"; see Evidence & Reproducibility. - Repeat a run : use Scheduled tasks for a single instruction and Create Loop for multiple steps. - Work as a team : confirm Identity & Access first, then go to Collaboration. - Extend model capabilities : Skills, MCP, and locally installed packages do not change the plugin list; see Skills, MCP, and Extensions. Maturity and boundaries - Each plugin's maturity follows Feature status and limitations; page text describes only the current implementation scope and does not present source registration as verified completion. - Paper Radar and OpenContent have left the current product line; related entry points in older docs and screenshots no longer represent available features. - The Remote SSH connection manager (registering labs, VPNs, and SSH targets) is not included in the open-source client; the open-source workspace location picker only switches between local workspaces and attached remote sessions. - Content Space currently uses a user-supplied SiYuan service as its main Provider; the local mock Provider is for testing only and is not a user feature. - Whether something can be installed from the Extension Marketplace depends on the app's current index; entries that are not listed or are blocked state the reason, which does not affect bundled plugins. Relation to other chapters - How the workbench organizes workspaces, sessions, and approvals: see Workbench guides. - Runtimes, models, and security boundaries: see Runtime and models and Permissions and security. - How these plugins fit together in a complete research task: see End-to-end cases.

en.title: Project DAG
en.description: Aggregate project goals, claims, review status, and decisions across sessions.
en.body: Project DAG Project DAG compiles the committed Evidence snapshots of several sessions in the same project into a project-level immutable snapshot by goal, scope, and policy. It answers “what does the whole project know so far, and which conclusions still need review?” It does not read raw chat and does not accept uncommitted source graphs; claims and evidence relationships inside a session remain the single source of truth in Evidence DAG. How to open it - Entry: the Project DAG panel on the right; resource navigation from a project, Goal, or Snapshot opens the corresponding view. - Target: the project that corresponds to the current workspace, along with its committed Evidence snapshots. - Prerequisite: the project has at least one committed Evidence snapshot, and both the Evidence and Project services are available. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- View the project-wide graph Open the panel and read the latest committed Project snapshot Project-level claims, findings, and review status Set a project goal Fill in the title and description under Project goal and click Save goal A new Goal version Aggregate new evidence Click Update now and wait for the task to commit A new Project snapshot and receipt See what needs attention Review the attention count, audit status, and review package A to-do list Return to session evidence Click Open Evidence DAG for session The evidence graph of that session View claim provenance Select a Claim to see the strongest provenance path, sources, L0–L4, and breakpoints Cross-layer provenance details and related decisions Typical workflow 1. Complete analyses in several sessions and commit a snapshot in the Evidence DAG for each. 2. Open the Project DAG, fill in the project goal, and save it. 3. Click Update now and confirm that the receipt moves through queued and running to committed. 4. Review the attention items and key Claims, jumping back to the source session to verify when needed. 5. For restricted sources, read only the redacted paths and breakpoints; do not try to bypass the access policy. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: committed Evidence snapshots, project graphs, Claims, audit records, and decision records. - Writes: project update tasks, Goal versions, and immutable Project snapshots; audits write only to a separate sidecar. - Approval or external effects: panel operations are limited to local project records; any publication or external delivery still requires Runtime authorization, which project policy cannot replace. - What it does not do: read raw chat, accept uncommitted source graphs, modify the graph directly from the audit page, or cache the content of Evidence snapshots. Known limitations - The current implementation consumes only committed Evidence snapshots; an upstream commit merely marks the project as needing a refresh and does not compile each item automatically. - When the Project view is closed, nothing is precompiled; to get a new view, update explicitly and wait for the persistence receipt. - After a new snapshot is committed, audits that are queued, running, completed, or failed on the old snapshot are marked stale, and old Findings never overwrite the new graph. - When any link is restricted by the access policy, the provenance path is redacted and fails closed, keeping only irreversible hashes, existence, level, and breakpoints. - The audit is a fail-open, read-only sidecar; an audit failure does not turn a committed Project task into a failure and cannot modify the graph directly. Related pages - Evidence & Reproducibility: the group overview and the recommended record chain. - Evidence DAG: the only evidence source for the project graph. - Research Dossier: turn project results into an external deliverable. - Workspaces and sessions: how several sessions share one project scope. - Permissions and security: the boundary between access policy and publication authorization. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-project-dag v1.0.7.

en.title: Research Checkpoints
en.description: Automatically turn each round of research conversation into a restorable, immutable checkpoint.
en.body: Research Checkpoints Research Checkpoints automatically record accepted and completed chat turns as immutable research checkpoints, preserving that round's research narrative, change reason, sources, declared files, compute runs, Git references, and any operations that remain untracked. It answers “where do I continue from next time, and what was the basis then?”; it stores research context and a restore position rather than the workspace snapshot recorded by Git Checkpoints. Artifact bytes and version identity are stored by Artifact Versions. How to open it - Entry: Research record for this turn in the session result card; the card also offers Open research dossier . - Target: completed chat turns in the current Runtime and session. - Prerequisite: automatic recording is on by default, the session is bound to a workspace, and v1 is created once the first turn completes. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Record each research turn automatically Complete a research chat normally and wait for the record to be saved An immutable checkpoint version Read this turn's record View the title, change reason, inputs, and outputs on the result card This turn's research summary Open an exact output Select an output under Exact output artifacts and click Open The corresponding artifact version Go to the full dossier Click Open research dossier The exact record in the research dossier Handle a version conflict Save again from the current version, or discard this turn's record A conflict-handling receipt Start or stop recording Use Start automatic recording / Stop automatic recording in the research dossier A new policy revision number Typical workflow 1. Open a session with a workspace and confirm that research recording is on automatically. 2. Complete a round of research and wait for the result card to show that the record is saved. 3. Check the status of inputs, outputs, reproduction, provenance, control, and evidence. 4. Stay alert to operations shown as untracked; do not treat ordinary terminal activity as controlled execution. 5. To continue, select a historical record in the research dossier and restore it as a new version. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: turn content, tool receipts, workspace file changes, Artifacts, compute runs, and Git references. - Writes: the checkpoint manifest and record bindings are committed as a new version; artifact bytes are still stored by Artifact Versions. - Approval or external effects: importing an old session, handling a conflict, and restoring as a new version all require confirmation; starting or stopping recording returns a new policy revision number. - What it does not do: silently backfill conversations from a stopped-recording period, promote Terminal, IDE, or PTY activity to controlled execution, or rewrite existing versions. Known limitations - The current implementation covers only accepted, completed chat turns; turns during a stopped-recording period are not backfilled. - Ordinary Terminal, exec_command , IDE, file watchers, Git diffs, and after-the-fact hashes count only as observations, and the related output stays untracked or incomplete. - Importing an old session keeps only the chat content; the record is permanently marked legacy / incomplete and carries a blocking provenance breakpoint. - New checkpoints are visible only within the workspace and cannot be exported by default; query parameters that look like narrative, URLs, or credentials are redacted, but this is not a general content-leak prevention system. - When a provider's delivery result is ambiguous, the record stays pending and fails closed; it is never assigned to a turn automatically. Related pages - Evidence & Reproducibility: the group overview and the recommended record chain. - Research Dossier: read records, control automatic recording, and restore historical versions. - Git Checkpoints: save a workspace Git snapshot rather than research context. - Artifact Versions: store the artifact bytes and versions that a checkpoint references. - Workspaces and sessions: how a session scopes recording. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-research-checkpoints v1.0.4.

en.title: Research Dossier
en.description: Turn the research question, inputs, methods, results, and limitations into a readable deliverable.
en.body: Research Dossier The research dossier is the reading- and delivery-oriented view of research: it opens one exact artifact version or compute run, then combines the read-only records contributed by each domain into a research narrative, key artifacts, reproduction status, and limitations. It stores no records itself and holds no current pointer, and it never substitutes the latest version for the exact record requested; the research process is recorded by Research Checkpoints, and evidence relationships are still maintained by Evidence DAG. How to open it - Entry: Research in the top toolbar; the right panel is titled Research as well; Open research dossier on a session result card binds to the exact version. - Target: an exact artifact version or compute run, not a vague “latest result”. - Prerequisite: a research checkpoint, an exact artifact version, or a compute run record already exists, and the session is bound to a workspace. The research dossier brings the research narrative, version position, trust summary, and the limitations to consider onto one reading surface. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Read a research record Open it from an exact version or a compute run Overview, key artifacts, and trust summary Inspect research limitations Review Limitations to consider and Breakpoints An actionable list of limitations Browse historical versions Load older versions in the Versions area The version list and the current position Compare or restore Use Compare exact version or Restore as new version A diff summary and a new current version Preview or export Use Open verified preview or Export Bundle V2 A verified preview and a portable bundle Manage automatic recording Start or stop automatic recording, or import earlier chats A policy revision number and legacy records Typical workflow 1. Complete a round of research and click Open research dossier on the result card. 2. Check the exact target and version position, expanding technical details when needed to view the Version ID and digest. 3. Read the overview, research sources, declared files, reproduction status, and limitations. 4. To trace back or roll back, compare exact versions or restore as a new version, and check the receipt from the owning domain. 5. Before delivery, export Bundle V2 and confirm that access restrictions and unverified items are clearly accounted for. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: exact records from owning domains such as artifact versions, research checkpoints, compute runs, evidence, and Git checkpoints. - Writes: the dossier itself writes no records; restore, import, and the recording switch are all delegated to the owning domain. - Approval or external effects: restore and legacy-session import follow the confirmation policy of the owning domain; exporting a Bundle writes workspace files and asks for confirmation. - What it does not do: keep a copy of records, own the current pointer, or fall back to latest when a record is missing or a digest does not match. Known limitations - Feature status is Partially available : the entry is registered, but content quality depends on whether the task produced checkpoints, artifact versions, and evidence records. - The dossier itself stores no records; when an owning domain is unavailable, only the corresponding block degrades, and the rest of the verified content remains readable. - An exact-identity or digest mismatch fails closed and is never replaced with the source, the current version, or the latest version. - Imported legacy sessions are permanently marked legacy / incomplete and keep a blocking provenance breakpoint. - Empty blocks and inapplicable compute, evidence, or review blocks are omitted; return to the Evidence DAG when you need the full relationship graph. Related pages - Evidence & Reproducibility: the group overview and the recommended record chain. - Research Checkpoints: the upstream source of the records and restore actions in the dossier. - Artifact Versions: the exact version source that the dossier opens and compares. - Evidence DAG: the complete in-session evidence relationships behind the dossier. - Feature status and limitations: how the Partially available status is judged. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-research-dossier v1.0.3.

en.title: Scientific Compute
en.description: Validate job cycles, audit events, and reproducible traces with a local deterministic baseline.
en.body: Scientific Compute Scientific Compute provides a local, deterministic baseline for the job cycle: submission, monitoring, result collection, and event traces all run against fixed local fixtures. It is meant to validate how research compute is recorded, not to submit real cluster jobs. It comes before "preparing real compute"; actual remote execution still goes to the terminal or your own compute environment. Opening it - Entry point: an Agent invokes the baseline task in a session; there is no standalone workbench panel today. - Applies to: global run state, not bound to any workspace. - Prerequisite: no scheduler, cluster account, or external service; a working Runtime is needed to make the call. What it can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Confirm the current compute provider Query status Local fixture with no real scheduler, and only four available scenarios Run a baseline Choose the success, blocked, rerun, or human-intervention scenario Job and trace IDs, final state, resource usage, and trace integrity validation Inspect the event stream Read the returned JSONL Events such as submit, start, monitor, complete, fail, or recover Demonstrate interruption and recovery Use the blocked or rerun scenario Explainable state transitions and fixture artifact summaries Current implementation scope: the local fixture Provider only. It does not submit external jobs and does not claim support for Slurm, PBS, Kubernetes, or cloud scheduling; for real remote compute, connect to your own environment through the terminal. Typical workflow 1. Query status first and confirm that the current provider is the local fixture and that no real scheduler is present. 2. Choose a scenario and run the baseline, recording the trace ID, job ID, and final state. 3. Check the event count, trace integrity validation, and the JSONL to confirm the event chain is complete. 4. For blocked or rerun scenarios, verify state and artifact information to understand retry and recovery semantics. 5. When you need real compute, switch to the terminal in your own environment and bring the command, environment, inputs, and results back into the session. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Read: provider status; does not read workspace files. - Write: writes nothing to the workspace; artifact paths and checksums are only fixture descriptions inside the baseline trace. - Approval or external effects: compute runs locally with no external submission, so it does not trigger approval. - What it will not do: execute command strings, connect to clusters, produce real scientific results, or use fixture state as a basis for job scheduling. Known limitations - Only four fixed scenarios; results are deterministic fixtures, good for validating traces and flows but not for assessing real performance. - Baseline traces are not persisted; if you need to keep them, save them explicitly in the session or artifact system. - No graphical panel, and no way to monitor real queues from the UI. - Blocked scenarios return fixture diagnostics, not the actual reason a real job failed. - Slurm, PBS, and Kubernetes automatic scheduling are not declared as bundled capabilities; see Feature status and limitations. Related pages - Workbench tools: how the terminal and remote entry points divide the work. - Remote and collaboration: connection boundaries for remote workspaces and external environments. - Life Science Preview: view structure and sequence files before and after compute. - Feature status and limitations: the current stance on scheduling and remote capabilities. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-scientific-compute v0.1.2.

en.title: Scientific Figures
en.description: Select files, describe the plot you want in chat, really run Python, and compare and accept candidate figures.
en.body: Scientific Figures Select files → tell the AI how to draw → review the result → accept when satisfied. Scientific Figures ties a text request, Python code, an actual run, and image versions together. To revise an image, just keep typing the change; you do not need to box, arrow, or pin anything on the image. This page was updated from real local acceptance of @sciforge/plugin-scientific-plotting 0.4.0-mvp.10 (2026-11-05). It was verified on macOS arm64, the DSH Runtime, and Python + Matplotlib; it describes the capabilities of the locally signed MVP and does not mean this version has been released to all users in the public marketplace. R execution is not implemented yet. For the actual steps and screenshots of multi-file cleaning, four-panel figures, missing-value matrices, and failure recovery, see Complex scientific figure case. Installing and opening 1. In Extensions → Marketplace , find the Scientific Figures package compatible with your SciForge version, check the publisher and permissions, approve the installation, and enable it. If it is not listed, the maintainer must supply a signed package and its installation source. 2. Open a writable local workspace and a DSH session whose model is configured. 3. Select Scientific Figures from the plugin picker in the right sidebar. The default Figure page contains file input, text input, and image preview. The machine needs a working Python and Matplotlib. The plugin does not install dependencies automatically; if Python is unavailable, Matplotlib is missing, or a run fails, fix the specific error in the run log first. Starting from data and code Data and code are the core of reproducibility; the image is the result of one run. Under New , choose one of two starting points: Starting point Must provide What happens next --- --- --- Start from data (recommended) Data file, plotting request The AI inspects the data, writes code, freezes the inputs, actually runs it, and creates the first figure. Existing data and code Data file, Python code, request Saves the existing code and a data snapshot, runs once to establish a baseline; an existing image can be used for comparison. After you click Start plotting , check the run in the session on the left; when it finishes, refresh and select the figure. Later, keep typing changes on the Figure page; you do not need to reimport every raw data file. text Read data/trend.csv, use time as the x-axis and response as the y-axis. Draw a blue line chart with units on the axes. Do not fabricate data. Freeze this step's data and code and actually run it; for later changes, generate a candidate first and wait for my confirmation. File selection is a workspace file reference, not a browser upload entry point. With only an image, exact data cannot be restored. A supplied source image is marked "user-provided, not yet verified" and linked to the saved code and inputs; no past successful run is fabricated. The result of an actual run is kept as a separate version. What is saved at each step Record How it is saved --- --- Data Each code version has its own input byte snapshot, original relative path, SHA-256, and length. Child versions copy the parent's frozen data by default and do not re-read mutable workspace files. Code and parameters Full source file, entry point, parameters, and parent relationship; old versions are not overwritten. Run environment Python/Matplotlib versions, implementation, interpreter name, platform/architecture, and a list of installed Python package versions. Runs and artifacts Each run uses a new ID and records state, exit code, length-limited logs, and PNG, CSV, TSV, JSON, and TXT outputs; every file has a path, SHA-256, and byte count. Environment rebuild files A successful run automatically saves _environment/requirements.txt (exact versions), environment.json , and REBUILD.md . History Code, data, runs, source images, and candidates are all kept; Version history lets you view earlier figures. Accepting only changes the current figure pointer. When you modify code without changing data, the frozen inputs are inherited by default. To use updated data, tick Re-read workspace data in advanced settings to form a new version. If data cleaning, filtering, or transformation should feed the next step, you must first save the result file and include it in the next version's input snapshot; the plugin does not automatically capture the whole workspace or arbitrary variables in Python memory. Rerunning a specific version uses the code, parameters, and data bytes saved with it; rewriting or deleting the old source file should not change the saved snapshot. The environment listing helps you check dependencies, but it is not a portable container, a package binary archive, or a complete lockfile, and it does not guarantee identical image digests across platforms. Saving analysis artifacts, pagination, and recovery The script writes cleaned data and statistical results to SCIENTIFIC_FIGURES_OUTPUT_DIR , where they are saved alongside the figure, for example cleaned.csv , summary.json , and rules.txt . CSV/TSV/TXT must be valid UTF-8 and JSON must be parseable; an error fails explicitly rather than treating a bad file as a successful result. The PNG limit remains 16 files, 20 MiB each, 64 MiB total; analysis files have a separate limit of 32 files, 8 MiB each, 32 MiB total. To use a saved file in the next step, combine the workspace-relative .scientific-figures/ with the output.path returned by the run and put it into the new code version's inputPaths . That step copies and freezes the input again, so you do not have to manually save the staging file elsewhere in the workspace. Only PNGs can be published as figures ; data files can still be selected to view their saved path and summary. Code and runs shows 20 summary entries per page by default; click More code versions / More runs to load more. Full contents and verification files are fetched only when you read a selected record. A corrupted entry shows a local error and should not block other pages or break the record entry point. Trusted results from a terminated process are saved first, then artifacts are collected and submitted; staging is cleaned up only after submission succeeds. Among runs that have not finished or were interrupted , only entries with a trusted process result offer Complete interrupted record : this reuses the original result to finish the submission without rerunning Python. Entries with no result, an unconfirmed stopped process, or a leftover lock need inspection; the plugin will not guess success, steal the lock, or retry automatically. Rebuilding the environment The _environment directory of each successful run stores: the exact package version list, Python/platform/architecture information, and instructions for creating a virtual environment and installing dependencies. Match the recorded Python implementation, version, platform, and architecture first, then follow REBUILD.md in a separate virtual environment. The plugin only generates files and does not install packages automatically. The pinned-version file is not a hashed package lock and does not include binaries, drivers, system libraries, original index URLs, or editable source. Packages may be unavailable during a rebuild, and byte-identical images are not guaranteed across platforms. Old runs keep only the records that existed at the time and do not backfill historical environment files. Modifying, comparing, and accepting Keep describing changes in text, for example "keep the data, change the line to blue, shorten the title." The AI should save a new code version, actually run it, and publish the output as a candidate figure. - Current figure / After change : inspect the current version against the selected candidate. When several candidates exist, switch between them with the Candidate dropdown. - Request acceptance : sends an acceptance request into the session and waits for the host's formal approval. After confirming the object, click Allow in the approval, and only then does the current figure update. - Keep current figure : rejects the selected candidate and keeps using the current figure. Generating, publishing a candidate, and formally accepting are three separate steps. An AI reply of "done" does not mean it has been accepted; go by the actual operation result. After acceptance, the source image and the historical code and runs are still kept. When a figure changes, old candidates may lose their baseline and need to be regenerated. Viewing code and runs Open Code and runs when you need to verify the process; ordinary plotting does not require reading this first. 1. Select a version and click Load version to view the Python source. 2. After editing, click Save and freeze code to get a new child version; the old code is not overwritten. 3. Click Run frozen Python to see run status, exit code, and output. Expand parameters, input paths, source comparison, environment, and logs as needed. 4. A successful output can be published as a new figure or as a candidate for an existing figure; before publishing a candidate you need to read and select the current baseline. You can also expand All versions and sources to go from a specific figure to its linked code and run records. Case: modify a line chart and formally accept it This is a real application acceptance case from 2026-11-05 ; the data uses demo values and does not represent a research conclusion. It verified "chat request → freeze code → actual Python → candidate figure → formal approval → restart recovery." 1. Prepare data and the request The existing line chart has an x-axis of [1, 2, 3] and a y-axis of [1, 3, 8] . Provide the existing Python file in the panel and ask it to save a new child version with the y-axis changed to [2, 4, 7] , actually run it, publish a candidate, and not accept yet. text Based on the current line chart's Python code, keep the x-axis, change y to [2, 4, 7], save it as a new child version, and actually run it. Publish it as a candidate figure first; do not accept automatically. 2. Verify the actual output Item Measured result --- --- New code version chat-mvp-v5-20261105 , parent relationship preserved Run chat-mvp-run-v5-20261105 Run result completed , exit code 0 Environment Python 3.14.7 , Matplotlib 3.11.2 Output PNG, 960 × 720, 31,384 bytes Candidate r-ee889dbf7bff5aa71d3732541fa9d5a6 The chat auto-attached image was verified for real in 0.4.0-mvp.6 : after re-reading that run, the image decodes and displays normally. The screenshot comes from the actual chat attachment and was not redrawn. 3. Confirm acceptance and check after restart Click Request acceptance in the panel, and the session triggers the host's formal approval. After approval, the document revision becomes 7 and the current figure points to that candidate; the original figure is still kept. Then quit and restart SciForge: the chat box, file entry points, and accepted figure all recover, and the image still loads normally. FAQ Symptom Resolution --- --- AI finished but the panel still shows the old figure Click Refresh and check the figure and candidate selection. Sending fails Confirm that a working DSH session and model connection are available; keep your input and retry once the session recovers. Python or Matplotlib unavailable Check the error in Code and runs , configure the right interpreter and dependencies, then retry with a new run. Image auto-attachment shows File not found Update to a compatible version that includes the 0.4.0-mvp.6 fix, and ask the AI to re-read that run. Error paths already saved in old messages are not rewritten automatically. Cannot accept a candidate Check whether formal approval completed and whether the current document/baseline changed; do not hand-edit approval fields. Run failed but you still want to publish an image Fix it and run successfully first; a failed run cannot be published as a formal candidate. Current scope and boundaries - Implemented: Python + Matplotlib, saving PNG and CSV/TSV/JSON/TXT artifacts, code snapshots, dependency pin files, paginated history, interrupted-submission recovery, figure linking, and formal acceptance. R keeps the executor boundary, but execution is not implemented. - Inputs are workspace files. After a successful plot you must refresh manually; local dependencies and the model service are yours to configure. - On-image boxing, arrows, circling, and pin annotations are no longer provided. Other separate extensions such as Visual Review are unaffected by this page's changes. - Local Python has write isolation, but that is not the same as prohibiting global reads or network access. Model requests are also subject to the data policy of the model service you use, so do not claim "data never leaves the machine." Only execute trusted code. - This case covers a representative local path and does not promise pixel-identical reproduction on every platform, Runtime, or environment. Related pages - Extension Center: installation sources, permissions, and enabling/disabling. - Runtime and models: prepare a working session. - Workspaces and sessions: confirm the file and task context. - Feature status and limitations: verified scope and release status.

en.title: SiYuan Notes
en.description: Connect your own SiYuan service to the workbench and archive traceable Markdown summaries after tasks finish.
en.body: SiYuan Notes SiYuan Notes connects a user-provided remote SiYuan service to the workbench as a full-page editor for reading, editing, and archiving research records. It is used in the organization stage after task execution, and you can also consult notes during a task. SciForge does not bundle the kernel or run or manage that service for you. How to open it - Entry: SiYuan Notes in the left sidebar opens the full-page editor on the right. - Target: the SiYuan service you run or subscribe to, along with its notebooks and documents. - Prerequisite: an accessible HTTP/HTTPS SiYuan address. If the service requires authentication, set the SIYUAN_API_TOKEN environment variable. SciForge does not start or distribute the SiYuan kernel with the app. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Connect your own SiYuan Enter the service address in Settings on the page and save it; leave it blank to use the installation default An editor session that persists across restarts Edit and browse notes Use the SiYuan interface directly in the full-page editor Document changes in SiYuan Archive task summaries automatically For a top-level Agent turn that finishes successfully and produces a final reply, SciForge writes an entry to a notebook automatically A Markdown document in SciForge 工作总结 , containing the request, final reply, time, and turn identifier Have the Agent write to a specific document Ask the Agent to save results to SiYuan and provide the title, notebook, and path The target document in SiYuan Typical workflow 1. First confirm in the SiYuan service that the target notebook exists and is writable. If authentication is required, prepare an API token and set it in the launch environment. 2. Open SiYuan Notes from the left sidebar and enter the service address in Settings. If the page reports an error, retry or open Settings to correct it. 3. Read or edit in the editor. Do not place sensitive content that should not leave the local machine into a remote service. 4. After an Agent task completes normally, check whether a corresponding record appears under SciForge 工作总结 . If the service is temporarily unreachable, records queue and retry. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: the SiYuan service address, notebook list, and document content. The API token is read only from the environment. - Writes: documents in SiYuan. Automatic archiving writes to a fixed notebook, while Agent writes follow the requested title, notebook, and path. - Approval or external effects: archiving is an automatic external write after a successful task and does not prompt each time. The service address, token permissions, and note content leave the local machine, so confirm this before use. - What it does not do: start or bundle the SiYuan kernel, provide a local private mode, save to another location when the service is unreachable, or write the token into the interface configuration. Known limitations - Server mode only: you must provide an accessible SiYuan service, and the address must be HTTP/HTTPS. - The Content Space Provider currently declares notebook discovery only. You cannot upload or download files or perform native document operations through Content Space. - Automatic archiving covers only successful top-level Agent turns. Intermediate progress, failures, cancellations, and continuous sub-turns are not archived, and it does not produce a second AI summary or claim that the task is verified. - Archiving writes to the fixed notebook SciForge 工作总结 and the /SciForge path; the notebook is created if it does not exist. Retries of the same turn use a durable receipt to avoid duplicates. - Local private mode, which would bundle and host the SiYuan kernel, was rejected because of AGPL redistribution obligations and is not an available feature. - When the service is unreachable or a write result is uncertain, pending records are kept locally and retried on the next task or at startup. Unconfirmed writes are not repeated blindly. Related pages - Content Space: how SiYuan connects as a Provider and its capability boundaries. - Collaboration: collaborative delivery and post-task local archiving are two different paths. - Permissions and security: external service addresses, tokens, and data boundaries. - Feature status and limitations: the capability scope of the first version. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-siyuan-content-space-provider v0.1.0.

en.title: Terminal
en.description: Run commands directly in the workspace, verify the results, and keep key output in the session.
en.body: Terminal Terminal puts the command-line environment for the current workspace in the bottom panel. It is suited to running scripts, checking logs, and confirming the status of long-running tasks. You type commands in the panel yourself; when the Agent runs commands in a session, it follows the Runtime's approval and sandbox policies. These are not the same authorization chain. How to open it - Entry: Terminal in the top toolbar, or Terminal in the bottom panel. - Target: the current workspace. The terminal process uses the workspace root as its initial working directory. - Prerequisite: a workspace is open, and the local or remote Workspace Host can start a system shell. - Tabs: a workspace can have multiple tabs (up to 8), with support for renaming, closing other tabs, closing all tabs, and restarting the process. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Run a one-off command Enter a command in a tab and press Enter Terminal output and the process exit status Watch a long-running task Keep the tab open and scroll through the ongoing output Task progress; closing the tab ends that terminal process Separate tasks Create and name separate tabs Command-line sessions isolated by tab Reproduce experiment steps Put the commands in a script, run it in the terminal, and record key output Commands you can run again, plus exit statuses Typical workflow 1. Confirm that the workspace shown at the top is the project this task should work on. 2. Open Terminal and run pwd and read-only commands first to confirm the directory, interpreter, and dependencies. 3. For commands that will write files, access the network, or install software, check the target paths, arguments, and recovery plan first. 4. Explain the purpose of the command in the session, and bring key output, exit statuses, or error messages back into the conversation. 5. Check the file state after the task. Copy terminal content you need to keep into notes or an artifact.
