Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: commands can read files, environment variables, and network resources that the current user has permission to access. - Writes: commands can modify workspace files and may also write outside the workspace. The working directory is not a filesystem sandbox. - Approval or external effects: Terminal does not prompt for each command. Operations such as installing dependencies, accessing the network, and overwriting files take effect directly under the current user's permissions. - Agent execution: commands started by the Agent are governed by its Runtime's approval and sandbox settings. There is no promise that all commands skip approval, and no guarantee that every command triggers a prompt. - Output retention: commands and output stay with the tab in the current workspace and are not kept after the tab closes. Results from Agent-started commands return to the session context with the tool call. - What it does not do: it does not automatically write terminal content into the conversation record. Closing a tab ends the corresponding terminal process, but switching workspaces does not automatically end terminals that are already running. Known limitations - Terminal processes in remote workspaces run remotely, and output is read through incremental cursors. Remote controlled terminals are pipe-based and do not claim full pseudo-terminal (PTY) compatibility. - The tab limit is 8. Closing all tabs collapses the panel, and unsaved screen content is not restored. - Command availability depends on the shell, PATH, and dependencies on the local or remote host. SciForge does not install missing tools for you. - Terminal scrollback is limited. Write important output to files or logs, and use persistent scheduling or logging for long-running tasks. - Content in the manual terminal does not automatically enter the Agent context. To inform the Agent, paste the necessary excerpts into the session or have it run the commands itself. Related pages - Workbench tools: how files, Terminal, Browser, and Computer Use divide responsibilities. - Workspaces and sessions: workspace locations and session state. - Permissions and security: approvals, credentials, and the scope of command effects. - Remote resources and collaboration: terminals and data boundaries in remote workspaces. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-terminal v1.0.1.

en.title: Visual Review
en.description: Annotate revision notes on an image, then replace the source image after human confirmation.
en.body: Visual Review Visual Review turns "this is wrong here" into structured feedback the Agent can act on. It sits between producing a figure and delivering it: you point out the problems and make the final call, the Agent generates candidate versions from the annotations, and the plugin saves the comments, review package, and acceptance record. Opening it - Entry point: Visual Review in the top toolbar opens the right panel; a specific review starts from an image in the session. - Applies to: raster images, generated images, edited images, scientific charts, or slide images in the current workspace. - Prerequisite: the workspace is available; one review document binds one source image, and opening from a versioned artifact validates the digest and byte length. Generating a candidate version needs a Runtime and an image-generation MCP; annotating and exporting a review package alone needs no external service. What it can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Point out what to change Annotate with Box , Arrow , Circle , and Pin , and fill in revision suggestions Structured comments Hand the feedback to the Agent Click Generate revised version ; the plugin saves the comments, exports the review package, and sends the revision request Candidate version Compare before and after Inspect the candidate with Before , After , Split compare , and Overlay compare A difference judgment Accept or reject Accept and replace or Reject A new version, or the source image kept as is Unify the visual style Choose a reference image in Image style detection A paper visual specification bound to the document Typical workflow 1. Open Visual Review from an image in the session and confirm the source image and workspace; if it comes from a versioned artifact, confirm the bound version. 2. Pick an annotation tool and mark the problem, then fill in a revision suggestion for each item; comments you have handled can be marked resolved. 3. Click Generate revised version . The plugin saves the comments as a review package and sends a constrained revision request in the current session. 4. The candidate enters the comparison view once it is ready. Check cropping, overlap, label legibility, and whether data and unannotated regions were changed by mistake. 5. When everything looks right, click Accept and replace ; to redo it, click Reject . After acceptance the source image is replaced, and the old image keeps a revision backup. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Read: workspace raster images, review documents, bound Artifact Versions, existing comments, and candidate versions. - Write: review documents and comments, review packages; on accepting a candidate, first commit an Artifact Version, then atomically replace the source image and keep a backup. - Approval or external effects: Accept and replace is destructive and must be confirmed; generating a candidate calls the Agent/image-generation chain and may incur model calls and costs. - What it will not do: generate or edit images itself; overwrite the source image before a candidate is accepted; parse document layout or vector source files. Known limitations - Supports bounded raster images only (common PNG/JPEG/WebP and similar); slides are reviewed as images too, with no element-level editing. - Candidate versions must be produced by the Agent/image-generation chain and pass candidate QA; this plugin offers no "edit the image directly" button. - A document currently shows only one active candidate version; to try another approach, accept or reject the existing candidate first. - After acceptance, downstream documents are not recompiled automatically; the plugin prompts the Agent to recompile and check references. Related pages - Scientific Figures: a separate chat-based Python plotting plugin that compares candidates in its own panel and requests formal acceptance; it does not require the on-image annotation tools described on this page. - Evidence & Reproducibility: acceptance produces a new Artifact Version. - Agent workflows: how revision requests return to the session and produce candidates. - Permissions and security: destructive operations and confirmation boundaries. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-visual-review v1.0.2.

en.title: Five-minute quickstart
en.description: Open a local project with SciForge and let the Agent complete its first read-only analysis.
en.body: Five-minute quickstart This guide walks you through opening a local project and having Codex analyze its top-level structure. The task uses Codex's read-only sandbox and compares Git status before and after. Claude Code's Plan mode works differently; see Configure the read-only sandbox. The workspace opens correctly, the Runtime responds, the Agent gives you a project overview, and file state is unchanged before and after the task. Before you begin Prepare the following: - SciForge is installed and running - A clean Git workspace; for non-Git projects, make a copy first - A working model access method is configured - The Codex Runtime is installed and configured Cloud collaboration and other team features require additional setup. For your first run, start with a local workspace. Step 0: Record a project baseline If the project uses Git, run this in the project directory first: bash git status --short Save the output. Ideally it is empty; if changes already exist, confirm they are unrelated to your walkthrough. For non-Git projects, work on a copy. Step 1: Complete model and Runtime configuration On first launch, SciForge walks you through choosing a Model API or a Coding Plan . Model access determines where requests get model capability; the Runtime determines which Agent executes tasks. Figure 1: Model access options in the first-launch guide; Coding Plan and Model API are two independent paths. Once you reach the workbench, open Settings from the bottom-left corner and confirm on the AI assistant page that the Codex command is recognized. Step 2: Set the read-only sandbox Go to Settings → AI assistant and, in the Codex configuration section at the top of the page, change File access range to Can only read files . If the interface shows “Can edit workspace”, do not start this tutorial. Wait until the setting shows as applied, finish the current task, restart SciForge, and start a new session. Figure 2: The file access range lives in the Codex configuration section. The value in the screenshot is “Can edit workspace”; before following this tutorial, change it to “Can only read files” in the same place. Writing “do not modify files” in the prompt does not create technical isolation. If a request to widen permissions or call a write tool appears during execution, stop and review the task first; this analysis does not need those operations. Step 3: Open a local workspace In the workspace location menu, select Local workspace , then open the project directory you prepared. Confirm that the project area on the left shows the correct directory name. After you start a new session, the input area appears at the bottom of the workbench. Figure 3: The current local workspace on the left and the input area at the bottom where you send your first task. Step 4: Choose the execution Runtime In the execution settings area at the bottom-right of the input box, confirm that it currently shows codex . This setting chooses who executes; the upstream model is still determined by the model access configuration. If the current Runtime is not connected, go back to Settings → AI assistant and check the command and sign-in status. Step 5: Send a read-only task Enter the complete prompt below: Look at the current workspace, list only the top-level files and directories, and explain in one sentence what this project might be. Do not modify files. Figure 4: The prompt, the current workspace, and the execution Runtime are all visible at once. After you send it, the Agent reads the project structure and performs a read-only inspection. Figure 5: The same session enters the running state, with the original task text and execution status still visible. Step 6: Check the result and file state When the task finishes, the result should list the project's top-level contents and give one bounded judgment about the project. Figure 6: The final answer in the same session; the result stays consistent with the prompt you sent. Run it again: bash git status --short Compare the output with the pre-task state. A read-only task should not add, delete, or modify project files. Git status does not list ignored files such as caches; for a complete check, also compare the file list and content hashes in the copy. What done looks like - The workspace opens correctly - The current Runtime responds - Codex's file access range is set to “Can only read files” - The Agent can read and summarize the project's top-level structure - The interface shows the sent prompt, the execution, and the final result - Git status is identical before and after the task Going further After your first task, you can send: Continue the read-only analysis. Explain what the main directories are for, the likely entry files, and the recommended way to start or test the project; list separately anything you cannot confirm from the source. Do not modify files or install dependencies. Next, read Runtime and model access or continue to the ECCITE-seq virtual cell case.

en.title: Configure the read-only sandbox
en.description: Configure Codex's read-only execution scope, learn how Claude's Plan mode differs, and compare Git status before and after a task.
en.body: Configure the read-only sandbox “Do not modify files” in a prompt is a task requirement; you also need to configure execution permissions. This page uses Codex's read-only sandbox as the onboarding path; the file scope option of the same name in Claude Code maps to Plan mode , and the two isolate work differently. Where the setting lives 1. Open Settings in the bottom-left corner. 2. Go to AI assistant . 3. In the AI assistant configuration card at the top of the page, find Codex . 4. Find the File access range dropdown under that Runtime and select Can only read files . 5. Wait until the setting shows as applied. To avoid reusing a running connection, finish the current task and restart SciForge. 6. Return to the workbench, start a new session, and confirm at the bottom-right of the input box that the executor is codex . The Permissions shortcut button at the top of the page points to the Computer Use configuration; the file access range lives in each Runtime's own configuration section. Figure 1: The screenshot highlights the file access range. The value shown allows changes to the workspace; for read-only tasks, select “Can only read files” in the same control. Executor What “Can only read files” actually means When to use it --- --- --- Codex Asks Codex for its readOnly sandbox and disables command network access inside that sandbox Suitable for the local file inspection in this tutorial; stop and review any request that widens permissions Claude Code Uses Claude Code's plan permission mode For analysis and planning; do not claim this gives the same filesystem sandbox isolation as Codex DSH Has no file access range option of the same name; its native shell tools are off by default and require individual approval once enabled Read-only guarantees depend on the capability configuration of the selected ACP session and should not be equated with the Codex sandbox This setting is not a unified read-only switch for all of SciForge, remote services, and other desktop apps. Permissions for MCP, remote commands, and Computer Use must be checked separately; the first task uses only the tools needed to read a local project. What read-only mode allows Typically allowed: - List directories and read text files - Search source code and configuration - View Git status and diffs - Run checks that do not write to the workspace - Provide analyses, plans, and recommendations Not allowed: - Create, overwrite, rename, or delete files - Install dependencies that write to the project - Run commands that generate caches, logs, or build artifacts - Modify the Git index, commits, or branches Whether a command is truly read-only depends on what it does, not on its name. Some tests and interpreters generate caches automatically; if a write fails in the read-only sandbox, change your inspection method rather than widening permissions just to finish the tutorial. Double verification In a Git project, run this before and after the task: bash git status --short Comparing Git status detects changes; it does not replace execution isolation, and it does not list files ignored by .gitignore . To strictly verify every file, use a copy of the project and additionally compare the file list and content hashes before and after the task. If the output changes: 1. Stop all further tasks immediately. 2. Open the workbench's Changes panel and inspect the specific files. 3. Do not automatically delete or revert existing modifications. 4. Determine whether the changes come from the task, from tool caches, or already existed before the task. Figure 2: The Changes panel shows the file differences involved in the current session; Git status should still serve as an independent baseline. When to switch to workspace write Switch to Can edit workspace only when the task explicitly requires generating scripts, tables, charts, or documents, and you have checked the plan and output paths. Write tasks should use a project copy or a clean branch, and you should review the changes afterward. Next: Collaborate with the Agent.

en.title: Runtime and model access
en.description: Tell Model API, Coding Plan, Codex, Claude Code, and DeepSeek Harness apart, and complete the minimal configuration.
en.body: Runtime and model access SciForge separates configuration into two layers: where models come from, and who executes tasks. Layer What it determines Where to set it --- --- --- Model access Whether requests go through a Model API or a supported Coding Plan First-launch guide or Settings → General AI assistant Runtime Whether Codex, Claude Code, or DeepSeek Harness (DSH) plans and invokes tools Settings → AI assistant , and the bottom-right of the input box Choose model access When you choose Model API , you provide a Base URL, an API key, and a model name; if the upstream protocol is uncertain, leave automatic detection on. Figure 1: The minimum fields for a Model API. The address, key, and model name in the screenshot illustrate the fields only; do not copy them. When you choose Coding Plan , complete authorization through the official sign-in or device code shown in the interface. The current implementation supports the Coding Plan path for Codex; Claude Code requires Model API access. A failed connection does not silently switch to the Model API. Configure Codex, Claude Code, or DSH Configure each Runtime separately in Settings → AI assistant : - Codex : selected by default; suited to general code, file, and tool tasks. - Claude Code : must be selected explicitly and configured with a Model API, and follows Claude Code's execution model. - DeepSeek Harness (DSH) : must be selected explicitly. SciForge checks the path you configured explicitly first, then PATH, then common install locations, and only falls back to the bundled DSH component if all of them fail; DSH's model and reasoning level take effect on the ACP session after connecting and are not changed here. DSH's native shell tools are off by default; once enabled, every execution still requires your individual approval. Typically keep the default command codex or claude . If automatic detection fails, enter the absolute path to the executable. Figure 2: The AI assistant page centralizes the command, the tool approval policy, and the file access range. Both Runtimes default to a Can edit workspace file access range. For your first read-only analysis, adjust Codex's range first; Claude's “Can only read files” maps to Plan mode and should not be treated as the same sandbox guarantee. For the steps, see Configure the read-only sandbox. When you want the Agent to operate desktop apps, continue on the settings page to check Computer Use 's Runtime access, Backend, and macOS permissions. Figure 3: Computer Use requires the Runtime, the Backend, and system permissions to all be in place. Choose the executor for the current session Back in the workbench, check the current Runtime in the execution settings area at the bottom-right of the input box. Switching Runtime does not carry over another Runtime's sign-in state, configuration, or session mapping. When the selected Runtime is unavailable, SciForge should show an error rather than switching to another Runtime automatically. Fix the current configuration, or switch explicitly yourself. Minimal verification Start a new session and send: Reply only with “connection successful”. Do not read or modify files, and do not call external services. Once you receive a clear response, continue to the Five-minute quickstart.

en.title: SciForge documentation
en.description: Start with your first safe task and work up to the research workbench, evidence chain, automation, and extension capabilities of SciForge.
en.body: SciForge documentation SciForge is an intelligent workbench for research tasks. It lets Codex , Claude Code , or DeepSeek Harness (DSH) execute tasks within explicit workspace, tool, and permission boundaries, while keeping files, commands, figures, evidence, and human review in a single workflow you can pick up again. This site is based on the public source code, generated capability catalog, and real interface of AGI4Sci/SciForge. Historical wikis, design drafts, or a single Agent answer are not treated as released features on their own. Recommended reading order Order Documentation set What you will accomplish ---: --- --- 1 Five-minute quickstart Complete your first local task in a read-only sandbox 2 End-to-end cases Understand how SciForge connects research questions, execution, evidence, and delivery 3 Features & Extensions Browse the 22 bundled domain extensions plugin by plugin, and learn about Skills, MCP, and the Extension Marketplace 4 Permissions and security Choose the right sandbox, approvals, and file access scope 5 Feature status Check which capabilities are verified, partially available, or experimental Four objects to understand first Object Role --- --- Workspace Points to a local or remote project directory and determines the file, Git, and terminal context Session Stores the messages, execution process, and results for a single goal Runtime Codex, Claude Code, or DSH handles planning, tool calls, and file operations Research record Pins results and their basis with artifact versions, Checkpoints, the Evidence DAG, and the Research Dossier How the documentation labels capabilities - Verified : The corresponding path has been completed against the current source code and real interface. - Partially available : The main entry point exists, but platform, data, or operational limits remain. - Experimental : Suitable as an integration or research direction; do not present it as a ready-to-use feature. - Not released : Exists only in designs, research drafts, or plans not yet implemented. For your first session, go straight to the Five-minute quickstart.

en.title: Documentation sync checklist
en.description: After a new public snapshot is released, verify the domain list, version numbers, retired features, and public boundaries, then update the documentation site and wiki.
en.body: Documentation sync checklist A maintenance checklist; it does not appear in the site sidebar. Intended for documentation site maintainers and export tool maintainers. Run this checklist in order after each new public snapshot of AGI4Sci/SciForge is released. The goal is not to “finish editing the docs,” but to keep the documentation site, the wiki, and the current snapshot's source code, interface, and domain list consistent, and to avoid writing non-public capabilities back onto public pages. 0. Record the baseline bash git -C <public-snapshot rev-parse HEAD git -C <public-snapshot log --oneline -3 - Record the commit in the “feature baseline” section of this repository's README.md and in each wiki page footer ( _Last verified: YYYY-MM-DD · public snapshot <sha _ ). - If the new snapshot only changed the README, links, or non-feature files, state “feature code unchanged” in the PR description and do not edit feature pages along the way. 1. Verify the domain list and version numbers bash for f in packages/domains/ /package.json; do node -p "const p=require('./$f'); p.name + ' ' + p.version" done - Compare page by page with the “Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-... vX.Y.Z ” note at the end of each docs/features/ .md page; version numbers must match exactly. - New domain: add the feature page, sidebars.ts , and the grouping table and count in docs/features/overview.md . - Removed domain: delete the page, the sidebar entry, the overview table row, and all internal links. - Counting rule: content-space-mock-provider is development-only and does not count toward the number of bundled domain extensions. The current public snapshot has 22 . - The page count is based on the plugin pages under docs/features/ and excludes the four landing pages overview , extensions , automation , and evidence-and-reproducibility . 2. Check retired features bash git grep -n "<功能名或包名 " -- src packages/domains packages/workers grep -v '\.test\.' - If only .test.ts , worker packages, or historical documents still reference it, the UI entry point has retired: remove the corresponding section, screenshot, and entry description from the documentation site, src/data/tour.json , README , and the wiki. - Keep one sentence in the “Maturity and boundaries” section of docs/features/overview.md — “retired from the current product line” — and do not keep operational steps. - Also check src/data/search-index.json : it is generated by the build script, so rebuild after changing the body text; do not edit it by hand. 3. Recheck public boundaries bash git grep -nE "remote-ssh Remote SSH VPN Zulip" -- docs README.md - Allowed: a one-sentence boundary note such as “this capability is not included in the open-source version.” - Not allowed: operational steps or screenshots for connection wizards, SSH target registration, VPN gateways, server deployment, or Zulip server adaptation. - Check the exclusion rules in the export tool sciforge-open-source-tooling/scripts/public-source-export.mjs : the excluded wiki pages and dead-link cleanup rules must match the current page set. - Do not change any repository visibility, publish a Release, or touch SciForge-cloud or SciForge-Zulip . 4. Update the documentation site and wiki - Documentation site: open a PR in AGI4Sci/sciforge-docs-v2 , one topic per page; merging into main deploys automatically. - English site: update the matching page under i18n/en/docusaurus-plugin-content-docs/current/ at the same time; when adding or removing a page, also update sidebars.ts and i18n/en/docusaurus-plugin-content-docs/current.json . - Wiki: make changes in docs/wiki/ of SciForge_client , then let the export tool sync them to the public repository; do not edit docs/wiki/ in the public repository directly, because the next export will overwrite it. - Unified feature-page template: positioning → how to open it → what it can do → typical flow → inputs, outputs, and permissions → known limitations → related pages. - Entry names must come from the snapshot's src/renderer/src/locales/zh/ .json and packages/domains/ /src/renderer/ messages.ts ; do not reuse wording from old screenshots. 5. Build verification bash npm ci npm run typecheck npm run build - onBrokenLinks is set to throw : any broken internal link fails the build, so a passing build means in-site links are reachable. - The search index is generated automatically before the build; confirm that src/data/search-index.json changed before committing. - If you changed a video chapter or narration script, also run node scripts/check-tour.cjs ; if the final video has not been re-recorded, do not change only tour-plan.cjs and claim the video is updated. 6. Deployment and live spot checks bash gh run watch curl -sI https://agi4sci.github.io/sciforge-docs-v2/ head -1 curl -s https://agi4sci.github.io/sciforge-docs-v2/docs/features/overview grep -o "<title [^<] " curl -s https://agi4sci.github.io/sciforge-docs-v2/docs/reference/feature-status grep -o "<title [^<] " - Spot-check three pages: home, features overview, and feature status (or the pages changed in this PR). - Confirm the deployment workflow succeeded and the live titles match the latest content; checking the local build/ alone does not count as release verification. 7. Wrap up - In the PR description, state: the snapshot commit, changed pages, verification commands and exit codes, and unfinished items. - List affected recording narration or visuals in a “needs re-recording” list; do not synthesize video inside a documentation PR. - If you find non-documentation files (such as INSTALL.md or DEVELOPMENT ) that do not match the snapshot, open a separate issue or follow-up PR; do not mix them into the documentation sync PR.

en.title: Remote resources and collaboration
en.description: Distinguish remote workspace sessions from SciForge Cloud collaboration, and understand the data and permission boundaries of each.
en.body: Remote resources and collaboration Remote workspaces answer “where computation and data live”; Cloud collaboration answers “who works together around a Project and Task.” You can combine the two or use either on its own. Remote workspaces A remote workspace brings a SciForge Workspace Host session running on another machine into the local workbench: files, the terminal, Git, and Agent requests act on the remote directory, while the interface stays on your machine. - Entry point: the Workspace location selector at the top of the workbench, which switches between Local workspace and attached remote sessions; the selector also shows each remote session's lifecycle (persistent Server / runs with the connection), connection status (remote, reconnecting, offline, limited functionality, connection error), and network egress. - When a session disconnects or errors, use Reconnect for that session in the selector. - The open-source client does not include a connection management panel for registering SSH targets, VPN environments, and workspace authorization; remote sessions appear in the selector only after a deployment provides and attaches them. Remote files, terminals, and Agent commands act on the remote directory. Do not mistake “shown in a local window” for “the data has been copied to this machine.” Remote workspace support may be narrower than local workspace support. Before using branches, snapshots, complex file operations, or scientific previews, check the feature status for the current version and validate in a test directory. Cloud collaboration Use Cloud collaboration when you need to continue a personal Session on your phone, or when a team needs to assign and accept Tasks around a Project. It requires a Cloud service address, account, and collaboration service configuration provided by your administrator. Team operation steps are in the Collaboration guide; a real request, rework, and downstream handoff are in the Pasilla three-person collaboration case. Check the sign-in and device prerequisites for team collaboration in that guide; setting up a personal Session on your phone is a separate path. Figure 2: Cloud connection status is independent of the local workspace. Unified sign-in has three distinct states: State Purpose --- --- Local account Marks the current user and ownership on this machine Cloud sign-in Confirms your cloud user identity Device connection Click Connect this device to authorize the current desktop installation to access Cloud capabilities A local account is not cloud authentication; a connected workspace also does not mean you have joined a collaboration Project. Figure 3: Team collaboration revolves around Projects, Tasks, owners, and acceptance results. Data and credential boundaries - SSH keys, VPN credentials, and MFA are managed by you or by system security infrastructure. - Cloud, collaboration services, and Content Space may send data to external services. - Before uploading production data, confirm the destination, scope, retention policy, and team permissions. - Remote commands and collaboration tasks should still record inputs, outputs, return codes, and approvals. - After a network interruption, check the state of the remote process before deciding whether to retry, so you do not submit the same computation twice. Case: Virtual cell perturbation prediction benchmark.

en.title: Permissions and security
en.description: Choose read-only, workspace write, approval, and Computer Use permissions based on the impact of the task.
en.body: Permissions and security Permission configuration should match the task goal. Broader permissions do not automatically make results better; they only widen the impact of mistakes or misuse. File access range Scope Suitable tasks Main risks --- --- --- Can only read files Project understanding, code review, data inventory, and planning Codex uses its read-only sandbox; Claude uses Plan mode, and the two are not equivalent Can edit workspace Changing code and generating analyses, figures, and reports Overwriting existing files, writing to the wrong directory, and mixing in unrelated changes Can access all files Controlled tasks that explicitly need reads or writes across directories Removes read-only or workspace scope limits and runs tools automatically, which may affect data and configuration outside the workspace Start first tasks, unfamiliar repositories, and unreviewed Skills from Codex's read-only configuration. Both Codex and Claude begin with a configuration that allows changes in the working directory, so you must adjust it yourself; MCP, remote execution, and Computer Use each need separate permission checks. For details, see Configure the read-only sandbox. Approval policy An approval request should state at least: - What operation will run - The target file, directory, host, or external service - Whether it will write, upload, send, or delete - Whether it can be retried safely after a failure - How to check the result and recover Denying approvals alone is no substitute for a read-only sandbox; default-allowed workspace writes may never trigger an approval at all. Credentials - Do not put API keys, tokens, or passwords in prompts, Git repositories, or screenshots. - MCP, the Model API, and collaboration services should each use the minimum credential scope they need. - Do not use a Provider key as a Runtime sign-in credential. - Before exporting logs, traces, or a research dossier, check for Authorization headers, server addresses, real paths, and sample privacy. Computer Use Computer Use may operate other desktop apps, so it is constrained at the same time by SciForge settings, Backend status, and macOS screen recording/accessibility permissions. Figure 1: Check the allowed Runtime, Backend, and operating-system permissions together before enabling it. The following actions should be confirmed by the user at the moment they run: account sign-in or authorization, sending messages, uploading data, purchases or payments, deleting external content, and submitting official evaluation results. Research data safety - Use public or redistributable data for tutorials. - Do not overwrite raw data by default; write derived results to a separate directory. - Whether data in a remote workspace may be downloaded is decided by project policy. - External models, MCP, and web uploads change the data boundary and must be evaluated separately. - Screenshots should hide real account names, keys, patient information, and server details. Pre-task checklist - [ ] The workspace or project copy is correct - [ ] A Git baseline has been recorded - [ ] The Runtime and file access range match the task - [ ] Output directories and overwrite policy are clear - [ ] Boundaries for network, installation, sign-in, and upload are clear - [ ] Acceptance and recovery methods are clear

en.title: Feature status and limitations
en.description: Distinguish SciForge capabilities that are currently verified, partially available, experimental, or not released.
en.body: Feature status and limitations This page is the first documentation baseline and does not replace the changelog for each release. Status comes from current source registration, user-visible entry points, and checks against the real interface. Capability Status Current notes --- --- --- Local workspaces and sessions Verified Open projects, create and continue sessions, and browse the workspace Codex Runtime Verified Default Runtime; configuration and sign-in failures report explicit errors Claude Code Runtime Verified Requires explicit user selection and Model API access; does not silently fall back to Codex DSH Runtime (DeepSeek Harness) Implementation verified Requires explicit user selection; model and reasoning level take effect on the ACP session, and native shell tools are off by default and approved one at a time Model API / Coding Plan Verified The API can be configured for Codex or Claude; the current Coding Plan path supports Codex Read-only and workspace write scope Implementation verified Both default to allowing workspace writes; Codex's read-only sandbox differs from Claude's Plan mode, and external tool permissions need separate checks File preview and Change Inspector Verified Supported formats and remote support differ Scheduled tasks Verified The app must be running, and the computer must stay awake when the task triggers Create Loop Verified Supports multi-node flows; paused approval state is not preserved across app restarts Scientific Figures Local MVP verified; no public release declared 0.4.0-mvp.6: file and text chat, real Python/Matplotlib, candidate previews, formal approval, restart recovery, and chat image attachments have been tested; requires a compatible signed package and local dependencies, currently accepted on macOS arm64 + DSH, R not implemented Artifact / Evidence / Dossier Partially available Entry points are registered; content quality depends on whether the task produces the corresponding records Remote workspace Connection management not included in the open-source version The Workspace location selector can switch between local and attached remote sessions; SSH targets, VPNs, and the authorization management panel are not included in the open-source repository Cloud collaboration Partially available Supports requirement confirmation, task delivery, rework, adoption, and closure; cloud sign-in and device connection are required first, see the Pasilla three-person collaboration case Extensions Center, Skills, and MCP Partially available Object types and security boundaries differ; some changes require restarting the session Virtual cell prediction models Not bundled Users can connect them through Agents, scripts, and external environments Slurm/PBS/Kubernetes automatic scheduling Not declared as bundled Current tutorials only describe using external environments through the terminal Status definitions - Verified : An entry point exists in the current version, and representative real operations have been completed. - Implementation verified : The source path from configuration to execution has been confirmed; this does not mean isolation testing is complete for every platform and tool combination. - Partially available : The main path exists but is limited by platform, data, Worker, external deployment, or sub-features. - Experimental : Suitable for controlled integration; do not promise ordinary users a complete closed loop. - Not bundled / Not released : Cannot be proven as a user-facing feature from source registration and the real interface. Documentation verification order 1. Whether the current source registers the capability. 2. Whether there is a user-visible entry point. 3. What the name and status are in the Chinese interface. 4. What the operation's Effect, Approval, and Scope are. 5. Whether it has completed one end-to-end verification in the real app. 6. Whether the screenshots come from the same version and the same task chain. When documentation and the product disagree, the actual behavior of the current release takes precedence; when filing an issue, include the version, entry point, reproduction steps, and redacted screenshots.

en.title: Troubleshooting
en.description: Diagnose SciForge problems across five layers — interface, Runtime, model access, permissions, and external services.
en.body: Troubleshooting First determine which layer the problem is in, so you do not change the model, Runtime, permissions, and workspace settings all at once. Five-layer quick diagnosis Layer Check first --- --- Application interface Whether SciForge starts normally and the current workspace is correct Runtime Whether Codex, Claude Code, or DSH is selected, whether the command can be found, and whether sign-in is valid Model access Whether the Model API or Coding Plan is fully configured Permissions and tools File access range, approvals, Computer Use Backend, and system permissions External services Whether Cloud, MCP, Worker, or Provider is reachable; whether a remote workspace session is still attached Runtime shows as disconnected 1. Open Settings → AI assistant and confirm the current Runtime. 2. In a system terminal, check whether codex , claude , or dsh can be found. 3. If automatic detection fails, enter the absolute path to the executable. 4. After the change, reconnect or start a new session. 5. Do not expect an automatic switch to another Runtime after a failure. Runtime is connected but the model does not respond - Confirm whether you are using the Model API or a Coding Plan. - The Model API requires a matching Base URL, API key, and model name. - A Coding Plan requires a valid official sign-in state. - The current Coding Plan path supports Codex; when you select Claude Code, configure Model API access. - Do not enter a Provider API key in the Runtime sign-in field. - Test first with a minimal prompt that reads no files, then investigate tools and the sandbox. Files still change during a read-only task 1. Stop the task immediately. 2. Compare git status --short before and after the task. 3. Open the Changes panel to check the files. 4. Confirm who executed the task, whether the setting was applied, and whether you approved a permission expansion; Claude Plan mode is not the same as Codex's read-only sandbox. 5. Check whether tests, interpreters, MCP, remote tools, or Computer Use wrote anything. Files ignored by Git need a separate check. 6. Do not automatically delete user changes that existed before the task. Scientific files are not understood - Check the extension, file version, and workspace reference. - Do not paste large files directly into the prompt. - Check whether the corresponding preview, Domain, or Worker is available. - If the current Provider does not support a binary format, degrade explicitly or stop; do not guess at the content. Evidence DAG or Dossier is empty These panels do not generate evidence automatically from an empty session. First have the task explicitly record the research question, inputs, methods, claims, sources, artifacts, and limitations, then refresh the corresponding panel. Remote workspace is interrupted - In the Workspace location selector, confirm the remote session status (remote, reconnecting, offline, or connection error). - Use Reconnect for a session that is offline or in error; if reconnecting fails, switch back to a local workspace and continue local tasks. - Check whether the remote command is still running, and do not submit a long computation again while the state is unknown. - After the connection recovers, check the logs, output files, and return codes. Include when filing an issue - SciForge version and operating system - The selected Runtime and model access method - Workspace type: local or remote - Minimal reproduction steps and when the problem occurred - Redacted logs or screenshots - Expected behavior and actual behavior Before submitting, remove API keys, Authorization headers, account names, server information, sample privacy, and real sensitive paths.

en.title: Collaborate with the Agent
en.description: Write tasks as goals, scope, constraints, and acceptance criteria, and check tools and approvals as execution proceeds.
en.body: Collaborate with the Agent A high-quality task is not a longer prompt. It is a shared understanding between you and the Agent of the goal, the allowed scope, the deliverables, and the stopping conditions. The four parts of an actionable task Part Question it answers Example --- --- --- Goal What problem should be solved in the end? Find the root cause of the failing test Scope Where may the Agent read and change files? Only the current package; do not change public APIs Constraints Which actions must not run automatically? Do not install dependencies or access the internet Acceptance How do you prove the task is complete? The relevant tests pass, and the root cause and changes are explained Recommended template: text Goal: ... Scope: ... Constraints: ... Deliverables: ... Acceptance: ... Stop if: ... Read first, plan next, write last For an unfamiliar project or research dataset, use three rounds: 1. Read-only analysis : Have the Agent establish a baseline for the project, the data, and the risks. 2. Plan review : Check the files to be changed, output paths, dependencies, and verification method. 3. Execute and verify : Switch to the appropriate permission, complete the writes, and review the diff. Figure 1: The original task text, execution status, and workspace stay visible in the same session. Inspect execution During execution, focus on: - The step the Agent is currently handling - The files it actually read - Tool calls and their parameters - Commands, return codes, and output - Files written and their target paths - Approval requests waiting for your decision An approval is not a “continue” button. Before you confirm, check the operation target, its impact, external destinations, and how to recover. Correct incomplete results Do not just say “be more detailed.” Point to the specific gap: You listed the entry files but did not explain the call chain from startup to the main interface. Continue the read-only analysis and list the functions and source paths in call order; label anything speculative separately. Split long tasks Split long tasks into phases that can be accepted independently, and write the inputs, outputs, and stopping conditions for each phase. Research tasks in particular should stop when a data audit fails, rather than continue producing figures and reports that look complete. Next: Workbench tools.

en.title: Workbench tools
en.description: Learn what the Files, Terminal, Browser, Computer Use, Changes, and research panels do.
en.body: Workbench tools The entries in the toolbar are scoped to the current workspace and session. Opening a tool does not authorize the Agent to perform the external operations inside it. Tool What it is good for Key checks --- --- --- Files and preview Browse directories and open text, spreadsheets, images, or scientific objects Path, file version, and whether the file is raw data Terminal Run commands and view logs and long-running task status Working directory, parameters, return codes, and write and network impact Browser Open local previews or research material URL, sign-in state, downloads, and external submissions Computer Use Operate desktop apps that need a graphical interface Target app, system permissions, and confirmation of critical actions Changes Review the file differences in the current session Changes that existed before the task vs. new changes Artifacts and Checkpoints Pin figures, reports, and phase state Inputs, versions, and restore points Evidence DAG / Dossier Review claims and sources and produce research deliverables Counterevidence, limitations, and unverified items Principles for using tools - Confirm the workspace location shown at the top first. - Terminal commands must state what they will read and write. - Browser downloads, account sign-ins, and form submissions count as external effects. - Actions in Computer Use such as sending, authorizing, deleting, and paying should be confirmed by the user. - Explain tool results back in the session; do not leave only a raw output snippet that cannot be located. Figure 1: Computer Use is available only when the Runtime, Backend, and macOS permissions all allow it. For permissions, see Permissions and security.

en.title: Workspaces and sessions
en.description: Use a workspace to scope the project and a session to preserve each stretch of continuous work.
en.body: Workspaces and sessions A workspace determines where the Agent reads files, views Git, and runs commands; a session stores the messages, execution, and results for one goal. A single workspace can have multiple sessions. Open a workspace 1. In the workspace location menu, choose Local workspace or a remote target that has already been configured. 2. Choose the directory that contains the paper, code, or data. 3. Check the project name on the left and the location status at the top. 4. Use a new session for a new goal; keep the existing session when continuing the same goal. Figure 1: The left side organizes workspaces and past sessions; the center is where you start a new task. View and reference files Open the Files panel from the top toolbar, expand directories, and preview files. When you want the Agent to focus on a particular file or directory, use the reference action the page provides instead of pasting long content into the prompt. Figure 2: The Files panel shows the current workspace contents and can add objects to the current task context. Manage sessions - Click a session name to continue an earlier goal - Use search to find past sessions - Archive sessions you do not need right now, and restore them from the archived list - Before deleting, confirm that important results are saved to the workspace or the research record - Do not mix unrelated research goals in one very long session Check file changes After a write task finishes, open Changes : 1. Confirm which files this session touched. 2. Open the diff and check additions, deletions, and modifications line by line. 3. Distinguish new task changes from workspace state that already existed before the task. 4. When you need a correction, reference the specific file and problem in the original session. Figure 3: The Changes panel reviews session modifications; project-level Git status should still be checked independently. A clear session opening Read the README, dependency configuration, and main entry points in the current workspace. First give the shortest path to run and test; do not install dependencies or modify files. List anything you cannot confirm separately. Related page: Collaborate with the Agent.
